title: Rosalind Franklin and the Shape of DNA
summary: The story of Rosalind Franklin, whose precise X-ray crystallography revealed DNA's double-helix shape, work whose importance to science took years to be fully recognized.
poll: Getting credit for your work matters more than doing the work itself.

versions.title: Rosalind Franklin Looks at Tiny Shapes
versions.text:
Rosalind Franklin was a great scientist. She was born in London in 1920. As a girl, she loved to read. She loved to learn.

She went to a big school. She was good at science. She learned to use X-rays. X-rays are rays we cannot see.

She looked at crystals. A crystal is a hard, neat solid. She shined X-rays on crystals. The rays made marks on film. The marks showed the shape inside.

Then she looked at DNA. DNA is tiny. It helps our bodies grow. She took a clear photograph of DNA. It showed a twisted shape, like a ladder.

People used her photograph. They built a model of DNA. This was a huge discovery.

She got sick. She died in 1958. She was just 37. But we still use what she found. Her work helped the world know DNA.

Rosalind Franklin was one of the most careful scientists of her time. People admired how precise her work was. She was born in London, England, in 1920. As a girl, she loved math and science, and she read widely and asked many questions.

She went to a big school in England, where she studied chemistry. She graduated with top marks. She became a skilled researcher in X-ray crystallography, a method that uses X-rays to study the shape of crystals and molecules.

When X-rays pass through a crystal, they scatter into a pattern called a diffraction pattern. Researchers study this pattern to work out the shape of the molecule hidden inside.

She first used crystallography to study coal. She worked at a lab in Paris, where she became known for her exact, careful marks.

Later, she moved to a school in London. She turned her crystallography skills toward DNA, the molecule inside our cells that carries plans for how living things grow.

Working with very thin fibers of DNA, she made an unusually clear diffraction photograph. It later became famous as Photo 51. It showed that the DNA molecule had a twisted, spiral shape. Her precise marks revealed the width of that spiral.

In 1953, two other scientists combined her photograph and her careful marks with their own ideas. Together, they described DNA's full double-spiral shape. This find is now seen as one of the most important in science.

After her DNA work, she moved to a new lab. She used X-ray crystallography to study the shape of viruses, tiny particles that can make people and plants ill.

She became ill and died in 1958, at only 37 years old. For years, few people understood how large her part in the find had been. Today, researchers know her precise, patient work was key to understanding DNA.

versions.title: Rosalind Franklin: Picturing the Shape of DNA
versions.text:
Rosalind Franklin was one of the most meticulous scientists of the twentieth century. She was a researcher whose careful work produced key evidence in the history of biology. She was born in London, England, in 1920. As a girl, she loved mathematics and science, and she constantly questioned how the natural world worked.

She attended a university in England. She studied chemistry and physics there, graduating with outstanding marks. This was despite the limited chances often given to women in science at the time. She became a highly skilled researcher in X-ray crystallography, a technique that uses X-rays to reveal the shape of crystals and molecules.

When X-rays pass through a well-ordered crystal, they scatter into a diffraction pattern. A meticulous researcher can study that pattern to calculate the precise shape of the molecule hidden inside.

Rosalind first applied her skills to the study of coal. She worked at a laboratory in Paris, where her meticulous measurements earned her a strong reputation. Later, she moved to a university in London. She turned her skill toward DNA, the molecule that carries the plan for how living things grow.

Rosalind worked for many months with thin, fragile fibers of DNA. She produced an unusually sharp diffraction photograph, later famous as Photo 51, along with a detailed report describing her calculations. It showed that the DNA molecule had a twisted helix shape, with an exact width and a regular spacing between its turns.

In 1953, two other scientists combined Rosalind's photograph, her report, and her measurements with their own ideas. Together they described DNA's complete double-helix structure, a discovery now seen as one of the most important in science. For many years, Rosalind's contribution to this discovery was largely overlooked. She received far less credit than the two scientists who published the final model.

After her DNA research, Rosalind led a small team of researchers. She studied the structure of several viruses, tiny particles that can make people, animals, and plants seriously ill. Her work on viruses was itself an important contribution, admired by the researchers who continued it after her.

Rosalind became seriously ill and died in 1958, at only 37 years old. Nobel Prizes are not given after a scientist's death, so she could not share in the prize later awarded for the discovery of DNA's structure. Today, her legacy is firmly established. Historians recognize her meticulous, precise work as essential to one of biology's greatest discoveries.

versions.title: Rosalind Franklin: Picturing the Shape of DNA
versions.text:
Rosalind Franklin ranks among the most meticulous, rigorous, and resolutely persistent scientists of the entire twentieth century, a researcher whose painstaking experimental technique yielded some of the most consequential evidence in the whole history of biology. Born in London, England, in 1920, she was, even as a remarkably young girl, an avid and voracious reader possessing a particular passion for mathematics and science, forever questioning how the natural world actually operated at its most fundamental level.

She attended a university in England, where she studied chemistry and physics and graduated with outstanding distinction, despite the considerably limited opportunities that were routinely afforded to women pursuing scientific careers during that particular era. She subsequently became a highly accomplished researcher in X-ray crystallography, an exceptionally demanding and exacting technique that employs X-rays to reveal the three-dimensional shape of crystals and molecules. When X-rays pass through a well-ordered crystal, they scatter into a characteristic diffraction pattern, and a sufficiently meticulous researcher can analyze that pattern mathematically in order to calculate the precise shape of the molecule concealed deep within.

Rosalind first applied her considerable crystallography expertise to the detailed study of coal at a research laboratory in Paris, where her meticulous, almost obsessively painstaking measurements earned her a formidable reputation among fellow scientists throughout Europe. Later, she relocated to a university in London and redirected her considerable expertise toward an especially consequential target: DNA, the molecule found within nearly every living cell that carries the hereditary instructions governing how organisms grow and function.

Laboring for many arduous months with extremely thin, fragile fibers of DNA, Rosalind eventually produced an unusually sharp diffraction photograph, later celebrated among scientists worldwide as Photo 51, accompanied by a meticulously detailed internal report describing her exacting calculations. It demonstrated unmistakably that the DNA molecule possessed a precisely twisted helix shape, and her painstaking measurements revealed both the exact width of that helix and the remarkably regular spacing between its successive turns.

In 1953, two other scientists combined Rosalind's photograph, her unpublished report, and her meticulous measurements with their own model-building efforts to describe DNA's complete double-helix structure, a discovery now widely regarded as among the most significant in the entire history of science. For many years afterward, Rosalind's essential contribution to this landmark discovery was largely overlooked by the wider public, and she received considerably less credit and recognition than the two scientists who ultimately published the completed model.

After completing her pioneering DNA research, Rosalind relocated to a new laboratory, where she led a small, dedicated team of researchers and applied X-ray crystallography to investigate the intricate structure of several viruses, tiny particles capable of causing serious illness in people, animals, and plants alike. Her meticulous work on viruses constituted, in its own right, a significant and lasting scientific contribution, one subsequently admired and further extended by the researchers who continued it following her untimely death.

Rosalind became seriously and irreversibly ill, and died in 1958, at merely 37 years of age. Because Nobel Prizes are never awarded posthumously, she could not share in the prize later bestowed for the discovery of DNA's structure. Today, however, her legacy stands firmly and permanently established: historians of science and researchers across the entire globe now recognize her meticulous, exacting work as absolutely indispensable to one of biology's greatest and most consequential discoveries.

HIGH.prompt: Explain why Rosalind Franklin can be called a meticulous scientist whose legacy was overlooked for years. Use at least three pieces of evidence from the article, and discuss both her contribution to DNA and to virus research.
checklist: I explained why Rosalind Franklin can be called meticulous, with at least three pieces of evidence.
I discussed her contribution to both DNA and virus research.
I organized my answer in clear paragraphs with transitions such as furthermore and however.
HIGH.modelAnswer:
Rosalind Franklin deserves to be called a meticulous scientist because of the painstaking precision of her work. She trained as a chemist, then became an expert in X-ray crystallography, carefully measuring diffraction patterns from coal and later from DNA fibers. Her famous Photo 51 showed, with exact measurements, that DNA has a twisted helix shape, and this evidence became an essential contribution to the discovery of DNA's structure in 1953.

However, for many years her contribution was largely overlooked, since the two scientists who published the final model received far more public credit and, eventually, the Nobel Prize, which cannot be awarded after death. Furthermore, Rosalind's meticulous methods did not stop with DNA; she went on to lead important research on the structure of viruses. Today, her legacy as a precise, persistent scientist is fully recognized, showing that credit for important contributions can sometimes take many years to catch up with the truth.
